Key Characteristics of Networks

The key characteristics of networks — structure, dynamics, and growth — can be applied to mind and memory.

Characteristic What it means Mind/Memory mapping
Nodes & Edges Elements (neurons, concepts) and the connections (synapses, associations) among them. Hebbian assemblies; associative links.
Topology Small-world (high clustering + short paths) and scale-free (hub-dominated) patterns. Efficient integration with hub vulnerability.
Emergence & Nonlinearity Global patterns arise from local interactions with feedback and inhibition/excitation. Recall, insight, and “Aha” dynamics.
Weights Connection strengths bias flow and recall. Synaptic efficacy; semantic association strength.
Modularity & Integration Specialised clusters bridged by long-range links. Domain-specific processing + global workspace.
Dynamics & Flow Propagation, delays, oscillations, attractors. Temporal context; pattern completion/separation.
Plasticity Change in weights/structure over time. Learning, consolidation, reconsolidation.
Feedback & Recursion Loops stabilize/amplify states and enable control. Attention, working memory, metacognition.
Robustness/Fragility Resistant to random loss; sensitive to hub failure. Graceful degradation vs. critical lesions.
Growth Preferential attachment creates hubs. Habits and frequently used pathways strengthen.

Notes

  • Small-world structure: short path lengths + high clustering — foundational to efficient communication in many real networks, including brains.
  • Scale-free degree distributions: hub formation via preferential attachment; explains robustness to random failure but fragility to targeted hub damage.
  • Hebbian learning: “cells that fire together wire together” — a core mechanism for weight change (plasticity).
  • Attractor dynamics: associative memory emerges from recurrent connectivity; relevant to pattern completion and recall.
  • Graph-theoretic brain analysis: demonstrates modularity–integration balance across structural and functional networks.
